source_text: Videamus nune breviter quid etiam de repromissionibus sentiendum sit. Certum est quia nullum animal omnimodis otiosum atque immobile esse potest, sed omni genere moveri et agere semper et velle aliquid gestit; et hanc inesse naturam omnibus animantibus manifestum puto. Multo ergo magis rationabile animal, id est hominis naturam necesse est semper aliquid movere vel agere. Et si quidem immemor sui sit eb quid se deceat ignoret, circa usus corporales omnis sua movetur intentio et per omnes motus suos erga voluptates ac libidines corporis oecupatur; si vero talis sit, qui in commune aliquid curare vel providere studeat, aut rei publicae consulens aut magistratibus parens aut quidquid illud est, quod in commune certe prodesse videatur, exercet. Jam vero si qui talis sit, ut aliquid melius quam haee, quae corporea videntur, intellegat et sapientiae ac scientiae operam navet, sine dubio erga huiuscemodi studia omnem sui declinabit industriam, quo possit inquisita veritate rerum causas rationemque cognoscere. Nicut ergo in hae vita alius quidem summum bonum corporis iudicat voluptatem, alius vero in commune consulere, alius studus et intellegentiae operam dare: ita requirimus in illa “vitae quae vera est, quae “abscondita essedicitur -cum Christo in deo’, id est in illa aeterna vita, si aliqui talis erii nobis vivendi ordo vel status. 2. Quidam ergo laborem quodammodo intellegentiae recusantes et superficiem quandam legis litterae consectantes et magis delectationi suae quodammodo ac libidini indulgentes, litterae solius discipuli, arbitrantur repromissiones futuras in voluptate et luxuria corporis exspectandas; et propter hoc praecipue carnes iterum desiderant post resurrectionem tales, quibus manducandi et bibendi et omnia, quae carnis et sanguinis sunt, agendi nusquam desit facultas, apostoli Pauli de resurrectione ‘spiritalis corporis- sententiam non sequentes. Quibus consequenter addunt etiam nuptiarum conventiones et filiorum proereationes etiam post resurrectionem futuras, fingentes sibimet ipsis Hierusalem urbem terrenam reaedificandam lapidibus pretiosis in fundamenta eius iaciendis, et de -lapide iaspide- muros eius erigendos, et propugnacula eius exornanda ex ‘lapide erystallo’; -peribolum- quoque habituram ex ‘lapidibus electis et variis, id est “iaspide et sapphiro et chaleedonio et smaragdo et sardio et onyce et chrysolito et chrysoprasso et hyacintho et amethysto. Tum etiam ministros deliciarum suarum dandos sibi “alienigenas- putant, quos vel -aratores- vel vinearum cultores. habeant vel ‘structores parietum”, a quibus diruta ipsorum et conlapsa civitas extruatur; et arbitrantur quod -facultates gentium aeeipiant ad edendum- et in divitiis eorum dominentur, ut etiam ‘cameli Madian et Gefar veniant’ et ‘afferant eis aurum et thus et lapides pretiosos. Et hoc conantur ex auctoritate prophetiea confirmare ex his, quae de Hierusalem repromissionibus scripta sunt; ubi etiam dicitur quia “qui serviunt deo manducabunt et bibent, peccatores autem esurient et sitient, et quod ‘laetitiam agent iusti, impios vero confusio possidebit. Et de novo quoque testamento vocem proferunt salvatoris, qua discipulis repromittit de vini laetitia dicens quia “non bibam ex hoe iam usquequo bibam illud vobiseum novum in regno patris mei”. Addunt quoque et illud, quod salvator “beatos- dieit eos, qui nune ‘esuriunt et sitiunt”, pollicens eis quia “saturabunturs; et multa alia ex seripturis exempla proferunt, quorum vim figuraliter vel spiritaliter intellegi debere non sentiunt. Tum vero secundum formam, quae in hac vita est, et secundum mundi huius dispositiones dignitatum vel ordinum vel eminentias potestatum “reges- se fore ‘et principes’ arbitrantur, sieut sunt isti terreni, propter illud videlicet, quod in evangelio dietum est: “Eris potestatem habens super quinque civitates”. Et, ut breviter dieam, secundum vitae huius conversationem per omnia similia esse volunt cuncta, quae de repromissionibus expeetantur, id est ut iterum sit hoe, quod est. Haec ita sentiunt qui Christo quidem credunt, Judaico autem quodam sensu scripturas divinas intellegentes, nihil ex his dignum divinis pollieitationibus praesumpserunt. 3. Hi vero, qui secundum apostolorum sensum theoriam scripturarum recipiunt, sperant -manducaturos- quidem -esse- sanctos, sed “panem vitae. qui veritatis et sapientiae cibis nutriat animam et inluminet mentem et potet eam divinae ‘sapientiae’ poculis, sicut dicit seriptura divina quia ‘sapientia praeparavit mensam suam, iugulavit vietimas suas, miscuit in cratere vinum suum et summa voce clamat: Devertite ad me et manducate panes, quos paravi vobis, et bibite vinum, quod miscui vobis”. Quibus “sapientiae- escis nutrita mens ad integrum et perfectum, sicut ex initio factus est homo, ‘ad imaginem- dei ac -similitudinem” reparetur: ut etiamsi quis ex hae vita minus eruditus abierit, probabilia tamen opera detulerit, instrui possit in illa Hierusalem civitate sanctorum, id est edoceri et informari et effici ‘lapis vivus”, apis pretiosus eb eleetus, pro eo quod fortiter et constanter pertulerit agones vitae et certamina pietatis; ibique hoe, quod iam hie praedictum est, verius manifestiusque cognoscet, “quod non in pane solo vivit homo, sed in omni verbo, quod procedit de ore deie. Sed et principes et rectores intellegendi sunt hi, qui inferiores et regunt et erudiunt et edocent atque instituunt ad divina. 4. Verum si minus haec videntur sperantibus ea dignum mentibus, ineutere desiderium, paululum repetentes, quam naturalis sit et insita animae rei ipsius cupiditas inquiramus, ut ita demum velut species ipsas “panis vitae- et qualitatem ‘vini eius’ ac proprietatem prineipatuum per theoriae consequentiam describamus. gitur sicut in artibus his, quae manu adimpleri solent, ratio quidem, quid vel quahter vel ad quos usus fiat, versatur in sensu, efficacla vero operis manuum ministerio explieatur: ita in operibus dei, quae ab eo facta sunt, sentiendum est quod eorum, quae videmus ab eo facta, ratio et intellegentia manet in occulto. Et sicut ea, quae ab artifice facta sunt, cum oculus noster viderit, si quid praecipue fabre factum perspexerit, continuo qualiter vel quomodo vel ad quos usus factum sit, ardet animus sciscitari: multo amplius et super omnem comparationem eorum, quae a deo facta pervidemus, ineffabili desiderio ardet animus agnoscere rationem. Quod desiderium, quem amorem sine dubio a deo nobis insitum credimus; et sicut oculus naturaliter lucem requirit et visum, et corpus nostrum escas et potum desiderat per naturam: ita mens nostra sciendae veritatis dei et rerum causas noscendi proprium ac naturale desiderium gerit. Accepimus autem a deo istud desiderium non ad hoc, ut nee debeat umquam nee possit expleri; ahoquin frustra a conditore deo menti nostrae videbitur ‘amor veritatis- insertus, si numquam desideri compos efficitur.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see briefly what is to be thought also about promises. It is certain that no animal at all can be completely idle and immobile, but it is necessary that it always be moved and act and desire something; and I think it is clear that this nature is in all living things. Therefore much more the rational animal, that is the nature of man, it is necessary always to move or act something. And if indeed he is forgetful of himself and ignores what is fitting for him, his entire intention is moved around bodily uses and through all his movements he is occupied with bodily pleasures and desires; if however he is such that he strives to care for or provide something in common, either consulting for the state or obeying magistrates or whatever that is which certainly seems to be of use in common, he exercises. Now indeed if someone is such that he understands something better than these bodily things and devotes himself to wisdom and knowledge, without doubt he will direct all his industry towards such studies, so that he may know the investigated truth of things and the reason. Just as therefore in this life one person judges the greatest good of the body to be pleasure, another to consult for the common good, another to devote himself to studies and intelligence: so we require in that life which is true, which is called hidden with Christ in God, that is in that eternal life, if some such order or status of living is for us. Then there are those who in some way reject the labor of intelligence and follow the surface of the letter of the law and indulge more in their own pleasure and desire, disciples of the letter alone, who think that future promises are to be expected in bodily pleasure and luxury; and because of this they desire especially to have flesh again after the resurrection, such that they may never lack the ability to eat and drink and do all things that are of flesh and blood, not following the opinion of the apostle Paul about the spiritual body of the resurrection. To these they also add marriages and the procreation of children even after the resurrection, imagining for themselves the earthly city of Jerusalem being rebuilt with precious stones in its foundations and its walls being raised from jasper and its battlements being adorned with crystal; and they think it will have a surrounding wall made of chosen and varied stones, that is jasper and sapphire and chalcedony and emerald and sardius and onyx and chrysolyte and chrysoprase and hyacinth and amethyst. Then they also think that they will be given foreign ministers of their delights, whom they may have as tillers or vineyard cultivators or builders of walls, from whom their ruined and collapsed city may be rebuilt; and they think that they will receive the riches of the nations to eat and will dominate in their wealth, so that even the camels of Midian and Ephah may come and bring them gold and frankincense and precious stones. And they try to confirm this from prophetic authority from those things that are written about the promises of Jerusalem; where it is also said that those who serve God will eat and drink, but sinners will hunger and thirst, and that the just will rejoice, but the impious will be possessed by confusion. And they also bring forth the voice of the Savior from the New Testament, in which he promises his disciples about the joy of wine, saying that he will not drink from this cup until he drinks it new with them in the kingdom of his Father. They also add that which the Savior says, that those who now hunger and thirst are blessed, promising them that they will be satisfied; and they bring forth many other examples from the scriptures, the force of which they do not think should be understood figuratively or spiritually. Then indeed according to the form which is in this life and according to the dispositions of this world, of dignities or orders or eminent powers, they think that they will be kings and princes, just as these earthly ones, because of that which is said in the gospel: You will have power over five cities. And, so that I may speak briefly, according to the conversation of this life in all things similar, they want all things that are expected from promises to be, that is so that what is may be again. These things are thought by those who believe in Christ, but understand the divine scriptures in a certain Jewish sense, and have not presumed anything worthy of divine promises. But those who receive the theory of the scriptures according to the sense of the apostles, hope that the saints will eat, but the bread of life, which nourishes the soul with the foods of truth and wisdom and illuminates the mind and inebriates it with the cups of divine wisdom, just as divine scripture says, that wisdom has prepared her table, has killed her victims, has mixed her wine in the cup, and cries out with a loud voice: Turn to me and eat the bread that I have prepared for you, and drink the wine that I have mixed for you. With which foods of wisdom the mind is nourished to integrity and perfection, just as man was made from the beginning, to the image and likeness of God: so that even if someone has departed from this life less educated, but has brought forth probable works, he may be instructed in that city of Jerusalem of the saints, that is taught and formed and made a living stone, a precious and chosen stone, because he has borne the struggles of life and the contests of piety strongly and constantly; and there he will know more truly and clearly what has already been predicted here, that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. But also the princes and rulers are to be understood as those who rule and teach and instruct and establish the inferiors in divine things. Truly if these things seem less worthy to those who hope for them, let us inquire, repeating a little, how natural and innate to the soul is the desire for the thing itself, so that we may finally describe the species themselves of the bread of life and the quality of its wine and the property of the principalities through the consequence of theory. Therefore just as in these arts which are usually fulfilled by hand, the reason indeed turns in the sense, what or how or for what use it is made, but the effectiveness of the work is explained by the ministry of the hands: so in the works of God, which have been made by him, it is to be thought that the reason and intelligence of those things which we see have been made by him remain in secret. And just as those things which have been made by an artisan, when our eye has seen them, if it has perceived something especially well made, immediately the soul burns to investigate how or in what way or for what use it was made: much more and beyond all comparison, the things which have been made by God, which we see, the soul burns with ineffable desire to know the reason. Which desire, what love we certainly believe has been implanted in us by God; and just as the eye naturally requires light and sight, and our body desires food and drink through nature: so our mind has its own and natural desire to know the truth of God and the causes of things. But we have received this desire from God not so that it may never be fulfilled, lest the love of truth seem to have been inserted in our mind by the Creator God in vain, if it is never satisfied.

pass_b_english: Let us now briefly consider what we should think about the promises as well. It is certain that no living creature can be completely idle and immobile; by nature it must always be in motion, acting, and desiring something. I regard it as clear that this impulse belongs to every living thing. Therefore, the rational animal — that is, human nature — must all the more always be moving or acting in some way. If a person is forgetful of himself and ignores what befits him, his whole intention is directed toward bodily needs, and through all his movements he is occupied with bodily pleasures and desires. But if he is the sort who strives to care for or provide something for the common good — whether consulting for the state, obeying magistrates, or practicing whatever else seems certainly useful in common — he exercises himself in that. Now if someone understands something better than these bodily things and devotes himself to wisdom and knowledge, he will without doubt direct all his industry toward such studies, so that he may come to know the investigated truth of things and their reason. Just as in this life one person judges the body's greatest good to be pleasure, another seeks the common good, and another devotes himself to study and intelligence, so we ask whether in that true life — the life "hidden with Christ in God" (Col 3:3), that is, eternal life — there might be some such order or status of living for us.

Some people, in a way rejecting the labor of intelligence and clinging to the surface of the letter of the law while indulging their own pleasure and desire, disciples of the letter alone, think that the future promises are to be expected in bodily pleasure and luxury. Because of this they especially desire to have flesh again after the resurrection — flesh that would never lack the ability to eat and drink and do all things that belong to flesh and blood — not following the apostle Paul's teaching about the "spiritual body" of the resurrection (1 Cor 15:44). Consequently they also add that marriages and the procreation of children will continue after the resurrection. They imagine for themselves the earthly city of Jerusalem rebuilt with precious stones laid in its foundations, its walls raised from jasper, its battlements adorned with crystal, and its surrounding wall made of chosen and varied stones: jasper, sapphire, chalcedony, emerald, sardius, onyx, chrysolite, chrysoprase, hyacinth, and amethyst (Rev 21:19–20). They also think that foreign ministers of their delights will be given to them — tillers, vineyard cultivators, builders of walls — from whom their ruined and collapsed city will be rebuilt. They think they will receive the riches of the nations to eat and will dominate in their wealth, so that even the camels of Midian and Ephah will come and bring them gold, frankincense, and precious stones (Isa 60:6). They try to confirm this from prophetic authority, from what is written about the promises to Jerusalem: that those who serve God will eat and drink, but sinners will hunger and thirst, and that the just will rejoice but the impious will be possessed by confusion (Isa 65:13–14). They also bring forward the Savior's voice from the New Testament, where he promises his disciples the joy of wine, saying he will not drink from this cup until he drinks it new with them in his Father's kingdom (Matt 26:29; Mark 14:25; Luke 22:18). They add, too, that the Savior called blessed those who now hunger and thirst, promising they will be satisfied (Matt 5:6; Luke 6:21), and they cite many other scriptural examples whose force they do not think should be understood figuratively or spiritually. Then, following the form of this life and the dispositions of this world — its dignities, orders, and eminent powers — they think they will be kings and princes, just like these earthly ones, because of what is said in the gospel: "You will have authority over five cities" (Luke 19:19; cf. Matt 25:21, 23). To put it briefly, according to the conduct of this life they want everything expected from the promises to be similar in all respects — that is, for what is to be again. These are the thoughts of those who believe in Christ but understand the divine scriptures in a certain Jewish sense, presuming nothing worthy of the divine promises.

But those who receive the theory of the scriptures according to the apostles' sense hope that the saints will indeed eat — but the bread of life, which nourishes the soul with the foods of truth and wisdom, illuminates the mind, and intoxicates it with the cups of divine wisdom. This is just as divine scripture says: "Wisdom has prepared her table, has killed her victims, has mixed her wine in the cup, and cries out with a loud voice: 'Turn to me and eat the bread I have prepared for you, and drink the wine I have mixed for you'" (Prov 9:2, 5). Nourished by these foods of wisdom, the mind is restored to integrity and perfection, just as man was made from the beginning in the image and likeness of God (Gen 1:26). So even if someone departs this life less educated but has brought forth probable works, he may be instructed in that city of Jerusalem of the saints — that is, taught, formed, and made a living stone, a precious and chosen stone, because he has borne the struggles of life and the contests of piety strongly and constantly (1 Pet 2:5). There he will know more truly and clearly what has already been predicted here: that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God (Deut 8:3; Matt 4:4; Luke 4:4). The princes and rulers, too, are to be understood as those who rule, teach, instruct, and establish the inferiors in divine things.

Now if these things seem less worthy to those who hope for them, let us inquire — repeating a little — how natural and innate to the soul is the desire for the thing itself, so that we may finally describe the species themselves of the bread of life, the quality of its wine, and the property of the principalities through the consequence of theory. Just as in those arts usually fulfilled by hand, the reason — what or how or for what use something is made — resides in the mind, while the effectiveness of the work is carried out by the ministry of the hands, so in the works of God, which he has made, we must understand that the reason and intelligence of those things we see made by him remain hidden. And just as when our eye sees things made by an artisan, if it perceives something especially well made, the soul immediately burns to investigate how or in what way or for what use it was made: much more, and beyond all comparison, the soul burns with ineffable desire to know the reason of those things made by God which we see. We certainly believe this desire — this love — has been implanted in us by God. Just as the eye naturally requires light and sight, and our body desires food and drink by nature, so our mind has its own natural desire to know the truth of God and the causes of things. We have received this desire from God not so that it may never be fulfilled, lest the love of truth seem to have been inserted in our mind by the Creator God in vain if it is never satisfied.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text, including the complex lists of gemstones and the theological distinctions between the 'Jewish' and 'apostolic' senses of scripture. All inline scripture citations in Pass B correspond correctly to the Latin allusions (e.g., the Proverbs 9 passage, the Genesis 1:26 allusion, and the Deuteronomy/Matthew bread of life reference). The translator correctly identified the specific biblical references required by the instructions.
